speakeroldname: Hon. Roberi Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement respecting the final payment on wheat. Producers delivered a total of 559,790,073 bushels of wheat to the Canadian Wheat Board in the 1965-66 crop year, which included 18,932,369 bushels of Durum wheat. The amount of the final payment to be distributed to producers is $270,028,575, which is $70 million higher than last year's payment and is exceeded only slightly by the record payment of $272 million made on the 1963-64 pool account, when a larger volume of wheat was marketed. Of this amount, $9,948,861 will be distributed to producers who delivered Durum wheat.
These sums are not a final payment by the government of Canada, but represent the net returns of the Canadian Wheat Board in the marketing of western Canadian wheat for the 1965-66 crop year.
The average final payment for wheat other than Durum is 48.087 cents per bushel. The average final payment for Durum wheat is 52.594 cents per bushel. The over-all average of 48.237 cents a bushel is the largest average final payment in the history of the Canadian Wheat Board.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
The board will commence issuing final payment cheques to producers on January 17,
23033-743J
1967. This is the earliest date on which final payments have been made in the last 14 years.
I wish to inform the house of the total prices realized by producers, prior to the deduction of the 1 per cent Prairie Farm Assistance Act levy, on their deliveries of some of the more important grades of wheat. The farmers will receive a total-basis in store at the lakehead of Vancouver-of $1.99699 for No. 1 Northern; $1.96645 for No. 2 Northern; $1.88269 for No. 3 Northern; $1.82731 for No. 4 Northern and $1.75100 for No. 5 wheat. The prices realized on the Amber Durum grades total $2.03725 for No. 1 C.W. Amber Durum; $2.00833 for No. 2 and $1.94476 for No. 1.
The accounting for the oats and barley pools for the 1965-66 crop year is under way, and distribution of the cheques will follow the distribution of the wheat payments. It is expected that the total of the payments for wheat, oats and barley will be at a record level.
Congratulations are due to all concerned in the growing, handling, grading, transporting and selling of wheat for their contribution to a most successful marketing year. I would like to pay particular tribute to the remarkable achievements of the Canadian Wheat Board. The efforts of the board on behalf of the western producer have benefited not only the grain producer but all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to table the statement issued today in Winnipeg by the Canadian Wheat Board regarding the final payment. I ask, if hon. members so wish, that it be included as an appendix to today's Hansard.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one time when we can all express pleasure, especially those of us on this side of the house; because during our period of office against strong criticism we made available to the wheat board
11750	COMMONS
Final Payment on Wheat the necessary credits tor guaranteeing sales to communist China. If it had not been for that we should have been back in the days of 1954 to 1957, when tremendous gluts of wheat piled up in all parts of western Canada.
Second, the tremendous sales this year bear out the prophecies we made that increasing amounts of wheat would be required for the world, and that the western farmer should expand his production and increase his acreage. When we expressed that view that too was criticized. Both these stands have been entirely vindicated by events.
The time has come for a material increase in price. I believe that $2.25 per bushel should be considered a normal price today. There is a growing world demand. One and a half years ago wheat prices in Canada were cut by some 17 cents a bushel. If that cut had not taken place the amount the western farmer would receive today would be approximately $130 million more than will be distributed on this occasion. I know the minister is most favourably disposed to action to increase wheat prices. That should be done. World demand is expanding by leaps and bounds.
While the western farmer will naturally be pleased with this distribution and the amounts realized, he is up against something that all farmers in all parts of our country are up against, rising costs of production.
This means that while these returns will be favourably accepted, the farmer is not yet receiving his just due, and it is necessary that action be taken in those fields in which the farmer has to make expenditures and in particular in the field of farm implements where prices have risen to untoward heights. While the commission sits, prices increase.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will want to congratulate the Canadian Wheat Board on the early distribution of the final payment to wheat producers. This has been a very prompt action, and it indicates the high degree of efficiency with which the Canadian Wheat Board conducts its operations. I am sure congratulations will be in order.
The final payment of some 48 cents on all grades of wheat except Durum, and 52J cents on Durum wheat, will of course be welcomed by the wheat producers of western Canada. The minister was wise, I think to point out once again to the general public the fact that this is not a payment by the government of Canada. This payment underlines the value of the orderly marketing of wheat under a government agency, something for which many of

DEBATES	January 13, 1967
us fought for a long period of years, and it is gratifying to see the degree of stability which this has provided for the wheat producers of Canada.
However, one thing which is sometimes lost sight of is that while wheat prices remain within a stabilised area, the cost of production borne by those who produce wheat has been rising steadily. I notice that in the publication "Canadian Farm Economics" issued by the Department of Agriculture last October the figure is given for the index of prices paid by farmers, excluding their living costs, and this is reported to have gone up from 282.2 in 1962 to 346.8 in April, 1966, the last date for which a figure is available. This represents an increase in the cost of production to wheat producers amounting to 64.6 points, a very substantial increase indeed. The same table shows that the prices paid to the farmers for field products, which includes products other than cereal grain though cereal grain is among them, went down from 191.7 in 1961 to 179.1 in June, 1966, a drop of 12.6 points. It is not necessary to tell this house that any industry in which the cost of production goes up by more than 64 points while the price received for that production goes down by 12.6 points is not in a very healthy position.
The producers of grain have been blessed with large crops. Nevertheless they face the problem of a cost-price squeeze. Certainly the time has come for Canada to press for an increased price in the negotiations for the renewal of the international wheat agreement. [DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
I might also remind the minister and the house that almost four years ago, in March, 1963 in the city of Saskatoon, the Prime Minister pledged that the Liberal party if it came to office, would establish a two price system for wheat with a guaranteed minimum price of at least $2 a bushel; that there would be a price set for the domestic wheat which would have some relationship to prices generally, and that this would enable the government to give the farmers a guaranteed minimum price. No action has ever been taken on this promise. I suggest to the minister that the time is long overdue for the government to carry out the pledge which was made by the Prime Minister almost four years ago.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of my party, I wish to join with the hon. members who spoke previously, and share in the joy of western farmers, following the announcement
January 13, 1967

which the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) has just made.
We, of the Ralliement Creditiste, as well as all the hon. members of the province of Quebec, wish to pay special tribute to the Canadian Wheat Board, to which we owe this tremendous accomplishment, and this group which brought pressure to bear upon the various governments, with a view to finding a market for their wheat.
We, of the province of Quebec, simply hope that the farmers in our areas will imitate the western efforts which were made a few years ago, in order to have such an organization, and thus force the governments into granting the farmers what they want because, in the province of Quebec, the problem is not so much one of production but rather of ability and opportunity to market their production at a profitable price.
I see that the western farmers, through the Canadian Wheat Board, have succeeded in performing that feat of calling on governments to help them, and 1 wish heartily that we may some day, in the province of Quebec, have such an organization that would be called the Canadian Eastern Products Board, in order that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might also announce payments for the province of Quebec and that the good news we hear might not always concern western Canada but also the farmers of the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, we wish to join the others who have spoken in expressing satisfaction that this final wheat payment is being made at this early date and in substantial amount. It will prove beneficial not only to the farmers of western Canada but to the entire economy of Canada.
There are only two brief points which I should like to make. In view of the political situation which is developing at present in red China I think there is concern in this country about markets for our wheat this year and next year, and whether shipments of wheat already agreed to will continue. This points up the necessity of expanding our markets in other areas of the world where food is just as necessary as it is in China.
It also brings out a second point, namely that the surplus of wheat and other food in the world today is decreasing, and the crisis of food for starving people in many parts of the world becomes more critical than ever.
Inquiries of the Ministry
It points up again the necessity of our own surplus supplies of food reaching areas of the world where we are not reaching today and where the needs are critical and urgent. It again comes back to the responsibility of the minister in respect of the necessity to not only develop our own production to greater heights, but also to develop new markets in the other parts of the world. This is something which is urgently facing us today.

I have a number of questions to ask the minister. Though through the years commissions have been appointed, we all know what has happened. We know that often the people did not get the hearing they ought to have had.
On the question of rail line abandonment I have a story to tell, a story about the mistreatment of the vast area I represent, a story of the treatment the people in my area received from the railway companies which fought at one time to get charters for the area. They fought for those charters and then, for many years, did nothing about them. My area has been unfairly treated.
Many people of my district, the veterans, the pioneers, have left. They waited for 40 or 50 years for the promised rail line; then being fed up with waiting, many left. Now in our centennial year we are threatened with abandonment of the line which really never was completed. We are threatened with the destruction of what we had hoped for. I am deeply concerned about this, and I wish to know the formula this commission will follow in considering what lines to abandon.
I have a story to tell; not many hon. members may have stories like this. I well remember the sod turning ceremony at Shellbrook, Saskatchewan, in 1928 for the building of the line that the company tries now to call a branch line. The project was never completed. If the line had been completed it would not have been a branch line but part of the main line on the north side of North Saskatchewan river serving the cities of North Battleford and Prince Albert, going through northern Saskatchewan on to northern Alberta and ultimately serving the entire territory north of the North Saskatchewan river. This line was never completed. Now the company applies to abandon this portion of line from Spruce Lake to Frenchman Butte so that it never will be completed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the proposed section 314C is the nub of the whole question of railway abandonment. I think the committee should have clearly in mind that the onus for making a case for railway abandonment must be laid squarely upon the railways. I feel that should be the basic assumption upon which all of this legislation is framed. The railways built these railways with public assistance in the form of financial grants, tracts of land with the mineral rights, and certain tax exemptions by both federal and provincial governments. These railways were built to give service to the people of the prairie provinces. The railways have done quite well financially. People have built their communities, their homes and their social activities around the railway centres.
Transportation
There is going to be tremendous economic and social disruption if these lines are abandoned. I am not saying that no line should ever be abandoned. It seems to me that in this committee we have to tighten this legislation as much as possible so that the onus is on the railways to prove to the satisfaction of the commission that the abandonment will not have adverse economic and social consequences upon the communities affected. It is not enough for the railway to be able to say that it is not making money on a particular line. It may be making money on other lines and often the branch line contributes to the profits which are being made on the main line.
It seems to me we cannot assume that mere proof by the railway it is losing money on a particular branch line should be adequate ground for permitting abandonment. It seems to me we have to be sure there is clearly written into this proposed section 314C the understanding that the railway must show that the community is not going to suffer adversely. Since we are about to rise for lunch, I will just ask the minister to give his views when we reassemble on subsection (1), lines 44, 45 and 46. These lines read in part as follows:
-determine whether the branch line is uneconomic and is likely to continue to be uneconomic and whether the line should be abandoned-
Are those to be the major criteria? I recognize that in subsection (2) other criteria are set out. However, I greatly fear that the restrictive criteria set out in subsection (1) may be interpreted to mean that the sole consideration will be whether the branch line is uneconomic and likely to continue to be uneconomic.

there is a threat to their railroad services, or the possibility of abandonment or reduction, they have misgivings about the possible future development of their areas.
When this bill was first introduced there was much concern in that particular area north of Guelph and extending to Kincardine, Southampton and Owen Sound because the history of railroad development in that area has been not too good during the last few years. As I indicated, most of those areas were originally developed as a result of the establishment of railway lines, the setting up of centres and the provision of stations and of facilities which would enable people to ship their products and to receive their supplies. When a few years ago the railroad reduced its service by cancelling the l.c.l. and the express service, and began to talk about removing stations, people began to wonder how long it would be before the railroad would cancel its services altogether. The situation was not improved by a statement which was made quite recently by the president of the C.N.R. in his year-end review, when he said:
While the legislation is not likely to provide any immediate financial benefits to the railways, it will when enacted remove outmoded restrictions and regulations which have hampered them in the past and place upon them the responsibility of paying their way in a highly competitive situation.
Such a statement does not allay the misgivings that a lot of the people have had with regard to railroad reductions and abandonments. Of course we know that for many years the C.N.R. has been talking about the necessity for more freedom in their operations, freedom in their costing and freedom in their ability to assist their own freight rates. However I think they are forgetting that freedom is something which is not easy to acquire these days. We have to live together in the world of today, and if one area develops faster than another then there must be some reason for it and assistance must be given to the underdeveloped areas to ensure uniform development. The railways started this. If they reduce many of their services they will automatically curtail development in many areas. As I said, this situation has created misgivings in many areas because the railroads in their operations over the years have not always considered the welfare of the area to be as important as those people who inhabit it thought it was.
We were very happy to hear the minister say today that every effort will be made to ensure that decisions will not be based solely on the word of the railway companies with regard to operational costs and revenues, but
Transportation
that the commission will have available independent expert opinion. Many of the municipalities will be relieved to hear this news. Some of us have attended meetings and have heard the railway companies presenting the costing figures, but we have had no way of examining them. We did not know exactly how they were arrived at and what part of the total figure was charged to the small municipalities. Without expert assistance it was very difficult to arrive at a proper conclusion and to present a proper case before the Board of Transport Commissioners in support of the retention of many of these facilities. In many cases the municipalities were not able to present their case adequately. However, the assurance which we received from the minister, that every effort will be made to make it possible for the municipalities to obtain satisfaction when applications for reductions or abandonments of lines are made, is welcome news to everyone.

I think the question of costing is quite important because if my understanding of the whole clause 42 is correct a railway must set out to prove that the cost of operating the branch lines is greater than the revenues obtained from running that service. As I have pointed out previously, the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. in presenting their cost figures on these branch lines attempted to prove that the situation is deteriorating and that the total revenue obtained from moving the grain on a branch line is not great enough to cover the costs of that operation. I think this point is very important and we should analyze each branch line separately.
I believe there is no reason why the revenue should be credited only to the branch line. It seems to me that part of that revenue could be credited to a portion of the branch line and the rest to the main line. There is no doubt in my mind that as a result of the abandonment

January 13, 19G7
Transportation
of some of these lines the farmers might find themselves closer to the other railway. For example if a C.N.R. line is abandoned, one which was normally used by farmers for hauling grain, they might find themselves closer to the C.P.R. line and therefore the C.N.R. might well lose the revenue. I believe therefore that an appraisal should be made of the original point at which the grain is shipped and of the line on which it travels. We cannot lose sight of the fact that the railways may consider that they might be better off without the grain.
In looking at their figures I noticed that in 1960 their revenues and expenditures balanced. That is not the case today. In fact since our grain trade has picked up in the last three or four years it is interesting to note that the revenues of the railways have also increased sharply. In presenting briefs with regard to rail line abandonment the railways have attempted to prove that they were losing money on the branch line. If that is the case, then it is logical to suppose that they are also losing money on the main line. If this is the case and the amount of grain hauled has increased, why have their revenues diminished?
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
If we go back about seven or eight years, for example, to the year 1957, we will find that the total export of wheat was something in the order of 256 million bushels, whereas last year it was 500 million bushels. It is logical to assume, if the railways are losing money on that grain trade, that their total revenue would be down rather than up. This is not the case. I have seen the figures which they have produced in respect of a branch line when they have attempted to prove that the *cost of moving the grain from the point of [DOT]origination on the branch line to the main line is greater than the cost of moving it on the main line to Vancouver or the lakehead. I think this method of proving the point is wrong. To my mind the railroads are making a profit in handling the grain through the main lines. I do not think the railroads would deny that, if there were no branch lines at all and just a main line running through the west, under the Crowsnest Pass rates they could operate and make a handsome profit. If they can make a handsome profit under the main line alone, then one would think they could operate a number of branch lines and still make a profit. The figures of the railways in a sense attempt to prove that they are making a loss on the main line.

There is another thing I should like to say in respect of grain movement and line abandonment. This has to do with the quota system. On many occasions the quota system works toward reducing the general efficiency in the movement of grain. I say this with the knowledge that the quota system is designed to allow farmers an equal opportunity to deliver their product to market and receive cash for it. One must consider, however, that in setting up a quota system one is influencing the cost of moving the grain to the lakehead. If in the opinion of the transport commission, when studying this branch line problem, it is necessary, economically and for the good of the community, that the branch line remain there, then I would suggest that they try to work out with the Canadian Wheat Board a better quota allotment for that branch line area. I realize that this would be a departure from the norm, but I believe it could be worked out. If the Canadian Wheat Board should find that in a particular branch line area there was the quality and quantity of wheat which was needed at the lakehead or Vancouver, I would suggest that instead of increasing the quota at one point on the branch line while other points remained at the unit quota they should advance the quota relatively equally on the whole line at the same time.
If there should be seven elevator points on a branch line and the railways are having difficulty moving grain out of that area through this branch line, because they are moving only six box cars at one time, which is uneconomical, then perhaps they could go in there with 26 or 36 empty box cars and go back a week later and move 26 or 36 full box cars out of that area. This could be done if the quota was moved up at all points on that branch line. I am bringing this up as one suggestion. If it were found that the railway was operating at a loss-and I am not for one moment accepting the railway's figures in this regard-and if the railway appealed to the commission that either a subsidy be paid or the branch line be abandoned, I would suggest that the commission should examine the possibility of working out with the Canadian Wheat Board quota allotments which would enable the railways to move that grain through the branch line in greater quantities. This would bring about greater efficiency in the overall movement of the grain.
Naturally I should also like the commission to take a look at the suggestion I made last evening with regard to truck transport. With
January 13, 1967

the modem facilities which we have today there is no reason, if they can move the grain more cheaply by truck, that the railways should not be permitted to do this. One other thing I whould like the commission to consider carefully in respect of the branch line abandonment is the question of storage. If the elevators along branch lines which are to be abandoned are not allowed to become line agents of the Canadian Wheat Board, then the prairie provinces will lose storage facilities for millions and millions of bushels. The elevator companies receive revenue from the storage of the grain and the grain is taken off the farmers' fields at a much faster rate than it would be with the loss of this storage. I do not doubt that in many areas of the prairie provinces at the present time one would find many farmers who have grain which is stored in temporary bins, or even outside where it is subject to weather and moisture conditions. This lowers the quality of the grain and does not help the farmer.
One has only to go back to the Bracken report in respect of box car allotment to recall what the elevator companies said at that time. At that time there was only one elevator company in the three prairie provinces which felt there was sufficient built-up storage in the prairies. All the others, although they may have said there was ample storage, said that they did not want to see the storage picture diminished to any extent, or something to that effect.
This whole matter should be looked into very carefully. I would hope that, rather than accept the straight dollars and cents calculation in respect of whether or not a branch line couild be abandoned the commission would take an over-all look at the whole picture to see whether somethiing could be done to improve the efficiency in respect of the handling of the grain.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
There is no denying the fact that the effects of the Crowsnest pass rates have been beneficial to the three prairie provinces, but when one sets up statutory rates certain conditions are not adjusted to meet future situations. Perhaps to some degree the elevator and railway companies have not been concerned about adopting up-to-date methods of handling grain.
Let me give an example. We were told by individuals who appeared before the committee that the C.N.R. tried to implement the use of huge hopper box cars. Only two elevator companies in Western Canada have elevators
Transportation
of sufficient capacity to fill those hopper cars, and there are only one or two terminals on the west coast which can handle grain delivered by the railway companies which use or did use these new cars for grain transportation.
While the Crowsnest pass rates have been beneficial to the prairie provinces-and let me hasten to add that they should be maintained at all costs-there is a growing fear that the railway companies and terminal operators have become stagnant so far as adopting better handling methods is concerned.
It is my hope that before the new commission accepts a flat dollars and cent cost in respect of the operation of branch lines it will attempt to persuade the elevator and railway companies to economize in other ways so that branch lines can be maintained for the social benefit of the community, and in order that their maintenance does not become a subsidized expense to the general taxpayers of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I will make a short statement.
The purpose of the bill is to allow an alternative means of incorporating companies without objects of pecuniary gain. These are, as will be found in the explanatory notes, corporations having objects of a national, patriotic, religious, philanthropic, charitable, scientific, artistic, social, professional or sporting character, or the like objects.
At the moment, Mr. Speaker, these incorporations must be brought before the House of Commons and dealt with in private members' hour, unless their membership is drawn from or their business carried on in more than one province, within the meaning of the present section 144 of the Canada Corporations Act. So that what it does is to open up an alternative procedure for incorporation. It allows
Canada Corporations Act Amendment bodies of this nature to go before the Registrar General's department by way of letters patent under an ordinary incorporation proceeding. The alternative of coming before parliament will, of course, still be open to them.
The reason this cannot be done now is that the words of the present section, as I have said, maintain that the purposes must envisage that the objects are carried on in more than one province of Canada. New words are now substituted, and they are "to which the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends".
Before the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Saumur case, it used to be thought that the parliament of Canada had no jurisdiction over, say, religious bodies unless they did carry on business in more than one province, because it was felt that the property and civil rights clause under head 13 of section 92 of the British North America Act gave the provinces exclusive jurisdiction and authority over religious bodies. Since the Saumur case it is now clear that the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, and these words are now changed to "to which the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends", replacing the more limiting words "carrying on in more than one province of Canada".

Legislative authority in respect of incorporation is, of course, divided between the dominion and the provinces. There are some kinds of corporations which can be incorporated by the dominion and cannot he incorporated by the provinces, and vice versa. Section 92 of the British North America Act, subsection 11, provides that the provinces have the right over-

There is no mention whatever of incorporation in section 91 except in subsection (15), which deals with the incorporation of banks. The King-that there is within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, and by delegation to the government of Canada, the power to issue letters patent covering corporations which I venture to suggest have authority in fields much beyond the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament.
In other words, I suggest that the position is that there is power in this parliament under its residual authority to invest in a corporation the status of a person, although the objects may be under the legislative jurisdiction of a province.
I should like to mention the type of corporation which has consistently been incorporated by letters patent under Part II, and which I think may well be now restricted by this particular legislation. subtopic: WHEAT BOARD STATEMENT RESPECTING FINAL PAYMENTS

speechtext:
The Canadian Wheat Board today announced the final payment on wheat delivered to the board during the crop year 1965-66.
Producers delivered a total of 559,790,073 bushels of wheat to the board in the 1965-66 crop year which included 18,369 bushels of Durum wheat. The amount of the final payment to be distributed to producers is $270,028,575 of which $9,948,861 will be distributed to producers who delivered Durum wheat. This is not a payment by the government of Canada, but represents the net returns of the Canadian Wheat Board in the marketing of western Canadian wheat for the 1965-66 crop year.
The average final payment for wheat other than Durum is 48.087 cents per bushel. The average final payment for Durum wheat is 52.549 cents per bushel.
The board will commence issuing final payment cheques to producers on January 17, 1967.
